learningObjective: Reason about how a runtime handles dynamic (unknown-at-compile-time) shapes: symbolic dim tracking, allocator reservation, and specialization vs generalization trade-offs.
stem: Which statements about how modern ML runtimes handle dynamic shapes are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A shape runtime maintains symbolic descriptors for tensor dimensions (batch = N, seq_len = S) and evaluates them at run time based on actual input shapes; downstream kernels can be parameterized on those symbols or specialized.

Compilers typically declare a set of shape ranges (min / opt / max, or bucketed shapes) at build time; runtime inputs falling within a supported range use the generalized kernel, while inputs outside the range typically trigger a fallback, recompilation, or error.

Fully-dynamic shapes and fully-static shapes are equivalent in cost: any modern compiler can generate a single kernel that is as fast on unknown shapes as on known ones, because dynamic-shape codegen has no runtime overhead versus fully specialized codegen.

Bucketing (grouping inputs into a small set of pre-compiled shape classes) is a standard practical trade-off: it retains most of the specialization benefit while covering a large range of real workloads, at the cost of build time proportional to the number of buckets.

explanation: A: symbolic dim tracking is the standard mechanism (torch.export's SymInt, TensorRT's dynamic dims, TVM's symbolic vars). B: shape ranges/optimization profiles are declared at build time and inputs outside them are not silently accepted. D: bucketing (padding inputs to canonical sizes or precompiling several bucket kernels) is a well-known deployment trade-off. C is wrong: dynamic-shape kernels typically have some overhead versus fully specialized ones (bounds checks, mask handling, less-tight tile shapes), and cost is not equal.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: symbolic dim descriptors are the standard tool.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: shape ranges must be declared at build.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: dynamic and static shapes are not zero-cost equivalent.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: bucketing is a mainstream practical technique.

assumptions: The runtime supports dynamic shapes (most modern stacks do to some degree).
nonImplications: Does not imply dynamic-shape kernels are always slow; the gap is often small for large ops.
Does not imply bucketing works for all workloads; extreme shape variability may exhaust the bucket budget.

performanceClaim.scope: Dynamic-vs-static kernel cost, bucketing trade-off in deployment
